description:
Team Outerstellar is building a burning activity calendar that combines MODIS and VIIRS satellite fire data.

MODIS and VIIRS are two satellites that detect fires, but their data can’t be compared directly. We’ll combine them using NASA FIRMS data into one consistent record. Then we’ll make a web app where users pick an area and see a color-coded fire calendar, compare the current month to the historical average, and download the results as a CSV.
summary:
The Harmonized Burning Activity Calendar is a web-based tool created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It helps people explore fire activity in Indonesia and Malaysia 25 years or more, from November 2000 to October 2026. 
This project uses active-fire data we search from NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System which also known as FIRMS, provided through Earthdata. Each record includes crucial information such as location, date and time. Then, the detections were organized into a monthly grid dataset with 75234 cell months records across 312 months. 
Our team uses an application method called harmonization method to make the two datasets more comparable, this method adjusts VIIRS counts to MODIS-equivalent values. Therefore, it helps create a more consistent view of fire activity across the change in satellite sensors. Users can select a region and date range, then explore the results through a year-by-month calendar. 
Ultimately, this tool is useful because fires and peatland burning in Southeast Asia can lead to haze which would affect people’s health, ecosystems and the climate. Thus, instead of having to work with separate satellite records, users can explore the combined information in one place and identify periods or areas that may need closer attention.
details:
Fire detecting satellites count burning on different scales so no one can tell whether this month’s fires in Southeast Asia are truly unusual or just counted differently. The Harmonized Burning Activity Calendar comes into action to fix it by converting NASA’S MODIS and VIIRS fire data into one consistent record from 2000 to 2026 so that anyone can observe whether a month’s burning activity is normal, high or even extreme. It allows users to pick a region such as preset, custom box or box drawn on the map and a month. It shows a Years X Months calendar heatmap which is coloured by hotspot count or by ratio to the historical median. It also flags unusual months and provides a simple situation brief and an alert banner in plain language. It also shows whether the current year is ahead of a normal season compared with the worst year on the record. Apart from that, it ranks all preset regions for the selected month and maps where the activity is unusual. The harmonization error and data quality notes are shown well to the users to know how far to trust each flag. The data is then exported into CSV, a one-page brief as well as an interactive HTML chart which is user friendly.

Fire detections are gridded into monthly 1° cells and low confidence detections are removed, MODIS is Terra plus Aqua and Terra only months before Aqua specifically July 2002 are scaled to match. From the year of 2012, VIIRS counts are divided by a factor k, estimated either once for the whole record (global) or separately for each calendar month (seasonal) to give MODIS-equivalent counts. Each month is compared with the same month in a baseline using default year of 2001 until 2020 using the interquartile range (IQR) rule whereby high is above Q3 + 1.5 X IQR, extreme is above Q3 + 3 X IQR and low is below Q1 – 1.5 X IQR. Not only that, but leave one year out validation measures the harmonization error and shows it clearly in the app. A flag is robust only if it still holds after allowing for a pessimistic, 80th percentile harmonization error. The months where a satellite reported on fewer than 90% of days are marked as data gaps. If the newest month in the data is incomplete in this way, it is never flagged.

Emergency responders and land managers get an instant and visual response to know whether there is any abnormal fire activity in plain-language and alert banner which is easily understandable. Besides that, scientists now have a transparent method. This is because the harmonization factor, baseline period and thresholds are all stated clearly and harmonization error is also measured and shown. A flag is only marked as “robust” if and only if it holds beyond that error. The months that a satellite reported on less than 90% of days are marked as data gaps so that they are aware for genuinely quiet periods too. Furthermore, the colour-blind-safe palette option and the plain-language briefs allows this app usable for both general publics. Moreover, this app is free of charge and needs only a web browser which is very convenient to use.

We hope to provide a trustworthy and consistent fire history since 2000 which can keeps running as MODIS retires, by bridging it to the VIIRS record. Besides that, we plan to add a near-real-time top-up so that the calendar will always stays updated and current. Next, we also wish to extend it to NOAA-20/21 VIIRS and more countries, then link all the fire seasons together to EI Nino to allow users predict the years that fire and haze might seriously occur.

Our project creatively bridges the scale mismatch between retiring MODIS and newer VIIRS satellite sensors, harmonizing NASA FIRMS data into one seamless 26-year fire history. To make the tool reliable, our team factored in seasonal cross-sensor variations, multi-decade historical baseline medians, and regional anomaly thresholds across Malaysia and Indonesia. Finally, we prioritized intuitive usability so emergency managers can spot unusual burning spikes and act on them at a glance.

The languages and libraries that we used in this NASA challenges are Python with pandas and NumPy for data processing and Plotly for interesting and interactive charts. Besides that, we also used Streamlit for the app framework. Next, GitHub is also used for coding and Streamlit Community Cloud is used for hosting. Moreover, we used NASA FIRMS active-fire-detections such as the MODIS and VIIRS Suomi-NPP as the data. In this hackathon, we didn’t use any special hardware.
projectRefs: Giglio, L., Schroeder, W., & Justice, C. O. (2016). The collection 6 MODIS active fire detection algorithm and fire products. Remote Sensing of Environment, 178, 31–41
